#2710. Game Recap: Saints host Browns in Week 9 clash

The New Orleans Saints were back in action after the bye week when the Cleveland Browns visited the Big Easy on Sunday afternoon. Here's a full recap of the matchup.

Cleveland began the game by going three-and-out, before Audric Estime got the Saints offense going straight away with three runs totalling 32 yards.

Tyler Shough then found Juwan Johnson for 19 more with his first throw, but a few unsuccessful runs and a sack later, the Saints were held to a field goal attempt.

Charlie Smyth converted from 30 yards to give the black and gold an early lead.

The Browns were then forced into another quick punt as the Saints defense got off to a strong start.

Shough found Chris Olave for 11 yards before breaking off for a 14-yard run, but it was soon another field goal attempt after he was sacked on 3rd down.

This time, Smyth was no good from 52 yards, and the score remained 3-0.

Shadeur Sanders found the first big play of the game for Cleveland with a 16-yard pass to Dylan Sampson, who also had a few short gains on the ground as the Browns drove past midfield.

After being stuffed short of the chains on 3rd down, a 41-yard field goal from Andre Szmyt tied the game.

Shough then copied a play from Paris with a 52-yard bomb downfield to Barion Brown as the Saints sought to regain the lead.

But a play later, Jordyn Tyson fumbled after making a catch, which the defense fell on to return possession to the Browns.

New Orleans was able to force another quick punt out of the Browns, but Brown fumbled on the return. Cleveland fell on it in the red zone.

A penalty against Carl Granderson helped the visitors set up 1st-and-goal, but he made up for it by sacking Sanders to push them back.

A few plays later, Sanders was just short of the goal line on 3rd-and-goal. The Browns offense stayed out there, and the Saints were able to come out big with a stop on 4th down to keep the game at 3-3.

Shough connected with Olave for 36 yards to move the Saints out from deep in their own territory, but after another pass for just one yard and two incompletions, they were forced to punt just before the half.

New Orleans went three-and-out and punted to begin the second half, before Sanders scrambled for 11 yards on 3rd down to avoid the same fate.

He then completed a 60-yard pass to Denzel Boston to set up 1st-and-goal.

But the Saints' defense came up huge once again, with a tackle-for-loss, sack, and incompletion from Sanders limiting Cleveland to a chip-shot field goal that gave them a 6-3 lead.

Shough responded with a scoring drive of his own, on a 54-yard drive highlighted by a 12-yard pass to Noah Fant and his own scrambles moving the ball down the field.

Smyth's 27-yard kick tied the game at 6-6.

Cleveland then went three-and-out as Granderson got to the quarterback once again, but New Orleans would do the same, which gave the visitors the ball to begin the fourth.

Sanders got the ball to midfield with a 10-yard pass to KC Concepcion, but failed to find another first down. He threw an incomplete pass to Sampson on 4th-and-2, and the Saints took over on downs again.

Taking advantage of the shorter field, Shough moved the black and gold into field goal range with a 9-yard throw to Tyson.

After being sacked by Myles Harden, the Saints were forced into yet another field goal, which Smyth converted from 48 yards.

But the lead didn't last long, as Sanders threw a 64-yard touchdown to Concepcion on the opening play of the ensuing drive to give Cleveland a 13-9 advantage.

New Orleans then went three-and-out, before Cleveland had another punt of their own around the two-minute warning.

Needing a touchdown, Shough found Olave for 33 yards to move the drive into the red zone. He then found Alvin Kamara for 8 more, before Estime ran in the 2-yard score to re-establish the lead for the black and gold.

But Sanders threw twice for a total of 37 yards to Jerry Jeudy, which set up a field goal that Szmyt converted from 51 yards to force overtime.

The Saints received first, and Kamara broke off three big runs as the ball moved past midfield.

Shough then found Devaughn Vele for 9 yards before Estime ran for 9 more.

Shough ran for 8 yards before finding Vele again, setting up a 15-yard touchdown throw to Johnson to give the black and gold a 23-16 lead.

Needing a touchdown of their own, two passes from Sanders to Boston helped Cleveland into Saints territory.

Sanders then found Harold Fannin Jr for a 39-yard touchdown.

Cleveland opted to go for two and the win, which is where the Saints came up with the biggest stop of the day as Sanders' pass intended for Boston fell incomplete.

New Orleans held on 23-22 to set up a huge divisional matchup next weekend with the Carolina Panthers.

#2704. Jonathan Taylor Trade Rumors: Vikings, Broncos, Packers among potential landing spots as deadline approaches

Jonathan Taylor is the talk of the town after the Colts shifted their stance on trading him. I'll be cataloging every trade rumor and update we get on the situation in this article, starting with a big update.

11/7 Update: The Ringer's Tom Pelissero believes Taylor is staying in Indy. The Colts are looking for a blockbuster haul and no team has made them an offer. This is by no means the end of the saga, but it's increasingly likely that the Colts' unreasonable ask for Taylor prices out all interested parties.

The Vikings make too much sense. They have possibly the best defense in the NFL and a weak passing attack. Given that a superstar quarterback isn't walking through the door anytime soon, they should be an old-school, ground-and-pound offense that complements the defense for low-scoring wins. They don't have the horses for that in their backfield right now. Aaron Jones has had a solid season while averaging 4.2 yards per carry, but he can't make it through a game without picking up a new injury. Jordan Mason, on the other hand, has missed time with an injury of his own and is plodding his way to 3.9 yards per attempt. Minnesota also has extra draft capital in 2027 via the Jonathan Greenard trade, which netted them the Eagles' third-round pick.

The Broncos were reportedly the team that nearly outbid the Texans for David Montgomery in the offseason. Jonah Coleman has emerged as a solid option for them, but RJ Harvey is on injured reserve and J.K. Dobbins—now relegated to backup duties—is averaging a dreary 3.3 yards per carry. Taylor would immediately take over as the workhorse back on a team that has failed to create a successful ground game for Sean Payton's entire tenure as head coach. Local reporter Zac Stevens makes it sound like they are pushing hard to get a deal done.

11/8 Update: NFL insider Josina Anderson says that the Giants have pulled out of conversations to acquire Taylor. Things change quickly in the NFL, but this sounds fairly definitive.

11/9 Update: While the Giants are reportedly out of the Taylor trade talks, their offer has been revealed. They were reportedly willing to part ways with second- and fifth-round picks for Taylor. The Colts declined, though that was likely to continue fielding offers. This might be the best deal they get. It would not be surprising for the Colts to circle back on this offer ahead of tomorrow's deadline.

Cam Skattebo's weird season makes the Taylor trade even more viable. He leads all running backs in fumbles and was benched after losing the ball in overtime versus the Commanders. Skattebo came back with a vengeance in Week 7 with a 17/124/1 rushing line, but he also went down with a hamstring injury at the end of the game. It held him out of Week 9's contest, though it looks like he will be back for Week 10. With his minor injury and Tyrone Tracy on IR, the Giants could view running back as a need regardless of the availability of Taylor. The fact that a superstar happens to be up for grabs is simply fortuitous timing.

The Packers are the last of the big four teams routinely linked to Taylor, including by NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, who didn't list the Seahawks or Bengals. Though that's simply pulling from the ticker on his Sunday morning segment.

11/9 Update: The Packers were already getting nothing out of their ground game, and now Jacobs is hurt. He has a fractured finger, though there's a chance he manages to play through it in Week 10. Still, Jacobs has been dreadfully inefficient this year and has ongoing legal troubles.

The injury could be the nudge Green Bay needed to pull the trigger on Taylor.

Schefter didn't specifically mention the Bengals in his Sunday morning hit, but NFL insider Jordan Schultz has included them as a team to watch.

Cincy's rushing attack is struggling this year. They are 22nd in EPA per rush attempt and Chase Brown ranks 38th in yards after contact per carry. Samaje Perine is shockingly ahead of him in that metric, though he only ranks 30th. The Bengals' defense has improved this year, but it's not going to carry them to a title. Their path to hoisting the Lombardi Trophy ultimately runs through having the league's best offense. Taylor would round out an offense that already has an unstoppable passing attack.

This destination continues to look less likely by the week. Schultz included Seattle in his list of teams interested in Taylor, but he's in the minority of reporters in that regard. The Seahawks just got first-round pick Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet back from stints on IR. Seattle trusts Charbonnet to do the dirty work and doesn't have much tape on Price because of the month he spent on injured reserve. It would be surprising for them to throw in the towel on Price after just four games.

At 4-4, they might not feel confident in pushing their chips in for the 2026 season either. The Giants at -160 (61.5 percent) are considerably more likely to make the playoffs than Seattle at -138 (58 percent), if you take DraftKings' numbers at face value. Seattle is undoubtedly a better offense when they have an elite running back to lean on. Given Sam Darnold's middling play this year, they are likely a team that benefits more than the average roster from a great running back. But their investment in Price and shaky start make a trade unlikely.

The Commanders stick out as a logical fit for Taylor, but reporters aren't bringing them up at all, so I'll keep this brief. Even at 2-4-1, they're still in the hunt for the NFC East crown. Their Week 10 game versus the Giants will have a massive impact on their place in the standings. With Jacory Croskey-Merritt on IR, Kaytron Allen waived, Jeremy McNichols potentially done for the year with a foot injury, and Jerome Ford waived, almost every notable member of the backfield is out of the picture. Rachaad White and Austin Ekeler are the last ones standing. For a team with a dynamic, dual-threat quarterback, the Commanders do not have a running back who can take advantage of the extra attention defenses pay to Jayden Daniels. The Commanders will likely do their due diligence regarding Taylor, but the lack of buzz connecting them to the trade talks likely means they're not in the running.

It's worth mentioning that the Colts aren't obligated to trade Taylor. Their asking price of a CMC-level haul could price all potential partners out.

Taylor is an elite runner, but McCaffrey's abilities as a receiver haven't been matched by anyone since Marshall Faulk. McCaffrey was also 26 when he was traded. Taylor is 27 and will turn 28 at the end of the regular season. There are enough interested parties and a desire to make this happen from the Colts' end that I bet a deal gets done, but it's not a foregone conclusion.

#2701. Warriors guard Will Richard out indefinitely with ligament tear in thumb

The Golden State Warriors announced some surprising news on the team's injury report for Monday night's game against the New Orleans Pelicans. Per the Dubs official release, second-year guard Will Richard is out indefinitely with a torn ulnar collateral ligament (UCL) in his left thumb. A 2023 study found that NBA players who suffered in-season thumb UCL tears missed on average 7.4 weeks of action (although there was a wide range of outcomes). Kings forward Keegan Murray suffered a similar injury last year and missed the first 15 games of the season.

Whether Richard is out for a month, three, or more, head coach Steve Kerr will now have a fourth player on the roster unavailable to him in the rotation. Richard joins Jimmy Butler, Moses Moody, and Kristaps Porzingis on the Warriors list of players with prolonged absences. Richard was off to a promising start to his sophomore NBA season prior to the injury, averaging 5.1 points and 1.8 rebounds on 47.5%/42.9%/80.0% shooting in 17.2 minutes per game across 10 games (3 starts).

The Warriors acquired Richard on a draft night trade back in 2025, acquiring his rights via the 56th overall pick. Richard had helped Florida win a National Championship in his final collegiate season and quickly made an impression in Golden State, looking like an early steal. Richard exploded for 30 points in his seventh NBA game and quickly became a mainstay in the rotation. However, he never again reached those heights and became a solid role player whose effectiveness ebbed and flowed with his jump shot.

Thus far this season, Richard was making his threes, but he was also continuing to show veteran savvy as a backcutter in the Warriors offense. Moreover, he was one of Kerr's go-to point of attack defenders against quick guards. Golden State already lacked point of attack defense, and the current roster does not have any obvious replacements for that component of Richard's role. Gary Payton II will likely receive more opportunities with perhaps a few minutes for two-way wing Malevy Leons.

#2700. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2695. Around the West: Sizing up the conference behind the Lakers

The Los Angeles Lakers have ridden a five-game winning streak to the top of the Western Conference with a 9-2 record. Luka Dončić is playing like the MVP, Austin Reaves looks like a legitimate All-NBA guard and a host of role players, headlined by Walker Kessler, are flourishing.

While a favorable schedule has benefitted them to some degree, wins count all the same and the Lakers are largely taking care of business, dismantling lesser teams in comfortable fashion.

But Los Angeles is not the lone team out West piling up victories. The four clubs directly behind them have won a combined 23 games in a row, led by the San Antonio Spurs' eight-game winning streak and the Golden State Warriors' seven-game winning streak. Early season standings are almost always jumbled, but the West is particularly unforgiving thus far. The Portland Trail Blazers began the weekend atop the conference at 6-1, then dropped a back-to-back set to the now No. 1 and 2 seeds and tumbled to eighth.

Moving forward, I'll regularly provide a snapshot of the Western Conference standings with a brief section on every team to offer a glimpse at the Lakers' fiercest foes.

Net ratings are courtesy of Cleaning the Glass and exclude garbage time.

Before November even arrived, the Thunder were dealt a trio of serious blows as three starters — Chet Holmgren, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace — all suffered serious injuries and are out for the foreseeable future. After a couple hiccups following a 4-0 start, they've rebounded to rattle off four straight wins.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is carrying the mantle as their engine while Ajay Mitchell instills crucial secondary creation. Rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz have also stepped up amid all the injuries to assimilate themselves and help keep OKC afloat.

The Spurs opened the year with a pair of losses and have since rampaged through the league. During their eight-game winning streak, six of their victories have been by double-digits, including five by 16 or more. They're the only team currently sitting top five in both offensive (third) and defensive rating (fourth). Victor Wembanyama is a two-way wrecking ball. Dylan Harper, now a starter, and De'Aaron Fox have flourished in complementary roles.

Their most pressing worry is Stephon Castle's slow start. He's struggled adapting to a greater off-ball role offensively, unable to burn teams from deep or attack the rim as often to draw fouls or finish inside. If he rediscovers his form of last year, they'll be even more potent.

Despite losing Anthony Edwards two weeks ago, the Timberwolves have won five of seven games — including four straight — in his absence. LaMelo Ball's wondrous shooting and playmaking have eased everyone else's burden offensively. Rudy Gobert continues to dominate defensively as a nearly unmatched interior defender. Ayo Dosunmu (18.1 points per game) and Jaden McDaniels (17.0) are stepping up to fill the void left behind by Edwards. The Wolves are rolling.

An 0-3 start to the year is already forgotten as Golden State's gone two weeks without losing. Over that span, they've scored impressive wins over the Timberwolves, Lakers, Miami Heat and Denver Nuggets. Stephen Curry is a supernova, averaging 31.3 points on 70.8% true shooting.

Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has proven himself a versatile front-court scorer — capable of posting up, spacing, rolling and handling — and paired aptly alongside Curry. Role players like Brandin Podziemski, De'Anthony Melton and Georges Niang are prospering. This team looks rejuvenated.

Having lost two straight, the Rockets are in a minor lull after a 5-0 start. They've benefited from Fred VanVleet's return and the arrival of Marcus Smart while Alperen Şengün (21-9-8-1-1, 59% true shooting) is loudly stamping his mark across games. Still a metronome of efficiency, Kevin Durant is averaging his fewest points per game (20.8) since his rookie year on a career-low 23.7% usage rate.

Subdued burst and ball-handling have limited his creation in recent years, so he's mostly a high-level play-finisher these days. It'll be interesting to see how Houston's offensive hierarchy and performance shakes out by season's end.

The Grizzlies are a well-rounded group led by Ty Jerome's full-fledged breakout. The veteran is averaging 26.6 points, 5.3 assists and 3.4 rebounds per game to power Memphis' surprising start. Rookie Cameron Boozer's passing and decision-making have popped but he's labored mightily to score the ball, shooting 33.9% overall and 35.8% inside the arc.

Remedying that means figuring out how to get to his spots without touting an overwhelming strength advantage. If he can become an effective scorer, he'll instill another valuable dynamic for Memphis.

Behind an array of complementary ball-handlers, some athletic and physical wing defenders and two imposing rim protectors, the Blazers have built a pretty nifty team. Fouls, turnovers and white-hot midrange shooting are sinking their defense (23rd overall) but they're second in offensive rating with a multifaceted attack.

They'll hope Ja Morant, who's currently out with a hamstring strain, can return as quickly as possible to further enhance their dynamic offense.

The Nuggets are still searching to find themselves early in the year, though they have won four of five. Nikola Jokić and Aaron Gordon have hardly looked like the terrifying forces of the past few years while the bench rotation hasn't established much rhythm.

Spencer Jones made his season debut this weekend. He'll help reinforce the wings. Christian Braun's off-ball scoring resembles that of 2024-25 rather than 2025-26, which is an encouraging development for Denver. Trevon Brazile and Bryce Hopkins might be nice finds as rotation players. Jamal Murray is humming as a scorer and passer. Matchups with Houston and Memphis this week will help illuminate the Nuggets' current quality.

Thus far, the Mavericks' big swing in hiring Dusty May from the collegiate ranks has paid off. He's established a movement-heavy offense that punishes gap help with cutting, relocating and snappy passing while utilizing all of the talent in the rotation.

Cooper Flagg is averaging 24-7-7-2 and playing like an early All-NBA candidate. Kyrie Irving's shooting and off-ball instincts have paired snugly next to the Mavs' budding superstar. Dallas should factor into the postseason conversation all year.

Peaks and valleys are the themes of the Pelicans' first few weeks. They opened 0-4, then ripped off four consecutive wins and followed those up with a two-game losing streak. Jeremiah Fears has improved as a driver and finisher. Saddiq Bey and Trey Murphy III chip in with versatile scoring from the wing spots.

New Orleans seems too talented to bottom out but too clunky and incongruent to truly compete for a playoff berth. We'll likely have a much better read on this team by December with another month of games under its belt.

Phoenix's busy offseason in which it revamped its starting five to land Miles Bridges has not panned out through three weeks. That starting group is disjointed and incompatible, lacking the passing, driving and defense to thrive. Second-year center Khaman Maluach has struggled, though shown some flashes on the offensive glass, as a finisher and defending the rim. Devin Booker is lighting up the nets, averaging 25.3 points on 59.9% true shooting.

Two wins in a row, most recently over the Rockets, has helped right the ship a tad. We'll see if they can keep the good vibes going on Tuesday against the Spurs.

The Clippers opened the year with a win over the Sacramento Kings before suffering seven straight losses, all of which came against postseason hopefuls or title contenders. Then, they knocked off the Pelicans Sunday night.

Darius Garland is scoring and shooting well (55.1% on 2s, 37.1% from deep) but is printing giveaways with 5.1 turnovers per game. Keaton Wagler is knocking down 39% of his triples and showcasing off-kilter craft to take 5.8 free throws each night (.712 free-throw rate) but cannot score inside the arc to save his life (28.1% on 2s). His development is the main priority this season.

One of four one-win teams this season, the Kings are mostly a mess. Darius Acuff Jr.'s passing and off-the-dribble scoring are among the rare glimmers of positivity. The rookie is averaging 25.9 points and 7.4 assists while showing a real knack operating in ball-screens. Following a tough first four games, he's also been pretty efficient, tallying 28.8 points and 9.2 assists per game while shooting 51.9% on 2s and 38.3% from deep (58.1% true shooting) over his last six outings.

It is fitting the West's most disappointing team will punctuate this week's debrief. The Jazz entered 2026-27 with genuine aspirations and have catastrophically flopped. They're on pace for their fewest wins and worst net rating since they began rebuilding in 2022-23.

Injuries are a factor. They dearly miss Jusuf Nurkic's screening and passing — a reliance on him is a blaring alarm bell on its own — and Jaren Jackson Jr. has only played four games. But Utah is too often scattered and stagnant offensively, cannot protect the rim and does not generate turnovers. There's lots of season left but the Jazz have hardly shown signs they're nearing a turnaround.

You can follow Jackson on Twitter at @jackfrank_jjf.

I hate to get so negative just one week into the season, but the Philadelphia Flyers have forced my hand. After a magical run to the second round of the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, the Flyers have fallen on their face through four games.

Philadelphia opened the season with a 7-0 loss to the rival Pittsburgh Penguins, and coach Rick Tocchet described his team's play as "disturbing." There was only one way for the season to go after that, right? Wrong.

The Flyers are off to an 0-2-2 start, and the underlying numbers aren't pretty. Per Natural Stat Trick, they have a five-on-five expected goals share of 26.0%, which ranks last in the NHL. Their 4.57 xGA/60 also ranks last. Their 1.94 xGF/60? You guessed it. Last.

Tocchet's bunch entered the season with a lot of well-earned optimism. Even with subpar play from Matvei Michkov last season, the Flyers managed to reach the Eastern Conference Semifinals. Rookie Porter Martone asserted himself as a budding star with six goals and nine assists in 19 games between the regular season and playoffs.

There's still plenty of time -- 80 games exactly -- for the Flyers to get back on track and restore that optimism, but to say this has been a discouraging start would be an understatement.

The Rays went 7-6 against New York during the regular season but lost four of the six contests at Yankee Stadium, including three of four in their penultimate series of the campaign. #2684. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2680. NBA Bracketology: Projecting the full 20-team postseason field as Knicks, Thunder take steps back

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA comes at you fast. One moment the Knicks are riding high off their first championship in 53 years, the next they're off to a sluggish start and scrambling to recover from losing their first three games. The Thunder went into the season rightly hailed as one of the deepest teams in the NBA — then had that assumption tested in harsh fashion after sustaining injuries to three of their five starters, with Jalen Williams (ankle and fibula) and Cason Wallace (shoulder) expected to miss most, if not all, of the season, and Chet Holmgren (knee) out at least two months.

While OKC suffered the most brutal blows on the injury front, the Thunder are hardly alone there. Several big name stars have already gone down and missed multiple games, among them Anthony Edwards (knee), Kawhi Leonard (knee), Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring), Jalen Duren (hamstring), Paolo Banchero (ankle), Jaren Jackson Jr (knee) and Ja Morant (hamstring).

The net effect is that an NBA season that was already expected to be competitive and wide open — particularly in the East, where the conference is as deep as it's been in recent memory — has been thrown into flux. While the Spurs and Thunder remain the betting favorites to win it all, the Sixers, Knicks, Celtics, Rockets, Raptors and Timberwolves are bunched up right behind them, with the Nuggets, Pistons, Cavaliers, Lakers and Blazers not far behind.

In the actual standings, the new-look Sixers have won seven of their first eight and are perched atop the Eastern Conference, while the surprising Memphis Grizzlies got out to a hot start in the West and were the last team in the league to lose their first game after getting upended by the Pelicans in overtime at home on Monday night. Meanwhile, Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Heat are under .500 and still trying to figure it out, while the Wolves and Warriors are just two teams out of several trying to stay afloat until key members of their respective teams return to the floor.

Various prediction models have differing opinions on what all this means in the long run. Those forecasts vary wildly, with one favoring the Raptors to come out of the East and another giving four other teams a better shot to win the conference than Toronto.

Predicting how all this will shake out in the end is difficult at best and folly at worst — so naturally that's exactly what we'll try to do over the course of the season.

This is our first installment of semi-regular NBA seeding predictions -- the NBA version of Bracketology -- where we'll give our best guess on where teams will be slotted once the playoffs roll around. The methodology is super scientific: watch a lot of basketball, consult with the mountain of stats and data available, and then eyeball it. Your mileage may vary.

Despite Duren playing all of 38 minutes this season, the Pistons have reminded everyone why they were the top seed in the East last season and have designs on something similar again this year. Detroit has proven to be a quality regular-season team, but the Pistons are still in desperate need of more shot creators and scoring to help ease the burden on Cade Cunningham. Their front office has work to do to level up the roster and avoid another disappointing postseason.

After what could charitably be called a tumultuous offseason, the Celtics once again look like a competitive, competent organization (apart from their struggles in Houston on Monday in the second night of a back-to-back) that figures to be a tough out in the East. Jayson Tatum is playing well enough to openly wonder "why not me?" when it comes to the MVP conversation, while Paul George's numbers to start the season look a lot more like the PG we saw in his final campaign with the Clippers rather than (mercifully for him and Boston) the lackluster version who was only intermittently available during his time in Philadelphia.

There were questions about the new-look Sixers going into the season, mainly how four big-name stars in the starting lineup would co-exist. The answer to date is that they've figured out ways to win when things have sometimes looked bleak. The Sixers lead the league in clutch victories, with six of their seven wins coming in games decided by five points or fewer with under five minutes to go. More surprising: they're top five in defensive rating and have allowed the second fewest points per game.

On paper, the Knicks have the best starting five in the NBA. That hasn't changed. Even though they didn't start the season looking like the dominant version of themselves that ripped through the playoffs en route to a title, the talent in New York remains undeniable.

The Raptors were a good defensive team last year and figure to be so again, but how far Toronto goes this season will be directly tied to Kawhi's availability — something that has been largely unknowable for much of the last decade of Leonard's career. As for the Cavaliers, their starting five is among the best in the league. After that, the roster gets thin and the questions begin to mount for Kenny Atkinson and the analytics team.

Maybe this is disrespecting the Hawks by lumping them with three teams that hardly inspire confidence, but the East feels like it has a solid six and then a pretty squishy bunch jockeying for play-in positioning. Miami fans won't like being in this group either — even though members of the Heat overreacted to their ugly start just like the rest of us and wondered aloud about the floor spacing and fit between Giannis and Bam Adebayo. Banchero is once again hurt in Orlando, but even when he's healthy, he and Franz Wagner (who is still searching for his elusive 3-point shot) have achieved exactly nothing together. The Wizards have been surprisingly plucky to begin the season, but if you're skeptical about Trae Young and Anthony Davis being on the floor enough to actually influence their record and help them sneak into the play-in, you aren't alone. Feel free to swap out the Hornets for one of these last-chance slots; Charlotte has been without the services of Kon Knueppel (hamstring) thus far and would undoubtedly benefit from his return.

Not pictured: the Pacers, who will be going nowhere fast if Haliburton and Ivica Zubac (ankle) don't get back on the floor sooner than later and stay there.

The Spurs are the biggest beneficiaries of the league-wide injury virus that has yet to infect them. The defending Western Conference champs are healthy, which is more than most teams can say. They still need to figure out the crowded and sometimes clunky backcourt fit between De'Aaron Fox, Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper, but as long as Victor Wembanyama is available, the West is once again theirs for the taking.

The Rockets were sorely in need of guard play last season after Fred VanVleet missed the season with a knee injury. He's back, and Houston has looked stout at both ends of the floor to begin the season (including Monday evening's comfortable home win over the Celtics). But is FVV's return enough to boost the Rockets and propel them to a deep postseason run, or does Houston need to make a move in a conference that is suddenly up for grabs outside of San Antonio? There will be endless rumors between now and the trade deadline about how the Rockets could use someone like Kyrie Irving — which does not mean the Mavericks will be keen on moving him.

If there's any team that could withstand losing three of its five starters for a significant chunk of the season, it's OKC. Sam Presti has done a masterful job making the Thunder into the deepest team in the league, but this represents the biggest challenge OKC has faced since developing into a perennial contender. How much weight can Shai Gilgeous-Alexander be reasonably expected to carry, and will guys like Ajay Mitchell, Isaiah Hartenstein, Alex Caruso, Jared McCain, and rookies Aday Mara and Bennett Stirtz be able to fill the void created in the absence of Williams, Wallace and Holmgren?

Luka Dončić is off to a scorching start, leads the league in scoring and has played better defense at times (and doesn't mind saying so himself), though even JJ Redick has openly questioned the roster and what the ancillary parts can be reasonably trusted with on a nightly basis. The Nuggets are once again thin after the starting five and are heavily reliant on Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray. And through the first five games, the Blazers boasted the third-best point differential in the league — but also lost Morant to a hamstring injury that will keep him out of the lineup for a while. At least it's Dame Time in Portland again.

There were those of us who doubted the fit with Anthony Edwards and LaMelo Ball and wondered whether the duo could make the Wolves into contenders — and that was before the team announced that Edwards would undergo an unexpected in-season knee surgery. That's asking Ball to do a lot in his absence. Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has played well and talked even better, but Golden State is still painfully thin while waiting for Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody to return from knee injuries (to say nothing of Kristaps Porzingis, whose status remains a mystery). Kyrie's name has been unsurprisingly floated in various trade rumors, but the Mavericks just might be competitive enough to entertain keeping him around. After moving on from Desmond Bane, Jaren Jackson Jr and Morant, the Grizzlies were supposed to be rebooting the franchise around rookie Cam Boozer. Memphis benefited mightily from a paper-thin schedule to start with wins over the Jazz (twice), Kings (twice), Warriors and Blazers before the Pelicans finally handed them their first L. It only gets harder from here — but even qualifying for the play-in would represent a successful season in Memphis.

#2679. Astros hire Randy Flores as new general manager as offseason filled with questions begins in Houston

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Houston Astros' search for a new head of baseball operations has ended with the hiring of Randy Flores as general manager. The 51-year-old Flores had been an assistant general manager with the St. Louis Cardinals. In Houston, Flores replaces Dana Brown, who was let go in late August. Flores becomes the fourth head of baseball operations to serve under Astros owner Jim Crane.

"Randy has had a huge impact on the Cardinals over the last 10 seasons," Crane said in a statement released by the club. "Throughout the entire interview process, we've been thoroughly impressed with Randy and his background in scouting and player acquisition. We're happy to welcome Randy and his family to the Astros and we can't wait to get to work on bringing another championship to Houston."

Added Flores: "I am excited and grateful for this amazing opportunity. The Astros have a long winning tradition under Jim Crane, and I look forward to contributing to the success.  I want to thank the Cardinals organization for the opportunities and support that made this next chapter possible. My family and I are excited to make Houston home."

Flores for roughly a decade served as scouting director for the Cardinals and was tasked with running their draft. He added the assistant GM title in 2018 and saw his portfolio of responsibilities expand within the last year.

Flores takes over an Astros organization beset by uncertainty. With an aging roster and after several key departures over the years, the Astros have seen their season-long win total decline for four straight years. This past season, the Astros eked out the American League Central title but finished with a .500 record and a negative run differential. In terms of success and roster strength, they're a long way from their dynasty years of 2017-22. It's not certain whether the Astros moving forward will try to squeeze out another season of relevance or embrace a rebuild, but either path will have its challenges.

Speaking of challenges, Crane and his trusted advisor Jeff Bagwell have been an increasingly meddlesome presence in recent years, and it's unclear to what degree Flores will have autonomy in his role. Whatever the future holds, Flores' first major decision is filling the managerial vacancy. After the end of the regular season, Crane opted not to renew the contract of former manager Joe Espada.

Prior to beginning his front office career, Flores spent parts of eight seasons in the majors as a left-handed reliever. In 2006, he earned a World Series ring as a member of that Cardinals team.

#2677. Ty Jerome is on a Linsanity-esque run, but here's why his MVP-level scoring isn't that big of a surprise

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Memphis Grizzlies finally lost a game on Monday night, their first of the year. But, of course, Ty Jerome was still the story. The Grizzlies point guard, who has gone full Linsanity Mode to start the season, rattled off 40 points on 64% shooting against the Pelicans. He made five of his six 3-pointers. He made seven of his eight free throws.

With the Grizzlies trailing 124-115 at the 1:43 mark, Jerome engineered a personal 9-0 run to close regulation and send the game to overtime.

TY JEROME HEATER TO FORCE OT!!! pic.twitter.com/kmet2W6esv

Less than two weeks removed from opening night (when Jerome put 45 on the Jazz), it's obviously too early to have a real MVP discussion. But, if we could, Jerome would be in it. The league's sixth-leading scorer, he's now averaging 28.3 points per game on 50/42/88 shooting splits.

People are wondering: how is this possible? Wasn't this guy a G League player? Yes, he was. But that was five years ago, and if you've been paying attention, you know he's been making consistent leaps as he has earned more and more opportunities. It's not to say anyone could've seen this kind of scoring boom coming, but there were signs.

Agfter bumping around with the Suns, Thunder and Warriors through the first four years of his career, Jerome, who had played well with whatever time he got specifically in OKC and Golden State, broke out with the Cavs during the 2024-25 season. He averaged 12.5 PPG on 51/44 shooting splits, finished third in Sixth Man of the Year voting, and became a legit go-to scorer in the playoffs.

In Clevaland's first-round sweep over the Heat, Jerome averaged over 16 PPG, making 10 of his 20 3-pointers and shooting 51% overall. In Game 1, he scored 16 of his 28 points on 6-of-7 shooting in the fourth quarter.

Look deeper at that season, and you'll see that Jerome was an All-Star-level scorer relative to his playing time, averaging 22.7 points per 36 minutes. That was a better mark that Jamal Murray, Tyrese Haliburton and Jimmy Butler, among many others. The only reason he wasn't a 20 PPG scorer was he only played 19.9 minutes per night on a Cleveland team that had Donovan Mitchell and Darius Garland ahead of him.

The Grizzlies saw this, and in the summer of 2025 signed Jerome to a three-year, $28 million contract that now looks like the biggest non-rookie bargain in the league. He only played in 15 games last season, but once again he was a per-minute monster.

After missing the first three-plus months to a calf strain, Jerome scored 20 points in 20 minutes in his Grizzlies debut, and over the following six weeks he averaged 0.87 points per minute played, the same mark as Kawhi Leonard and fourth-best in the league among players who logged at least 10 games.

The evidence was clear: If Jerome is on the court, he's going to score. It's just a matter of playing time. So far this season, he's playing 30 minutes per night, and is currently scoring 0.91 points in each of those minutes. That registers as the fourth-best mark in the league among players who have played at least 100 minutes.

It's not to say we should've seen an MVP-level start coming for Jerome, but at the same time this scoring wave he's currently riding didn't come out of nowhere. The signs trace back to Cleveland. As his minutes, and usage, have gone up, so too has his scoring. He is simply playing more minutes now with a 31.3% usage rate equal to Jalen Brunson.

Again, that's not to say Jerome is a superstar. But don't be thrown off by his underdog story or his lack of NBA athleticism. He's extraordinarily skilled and always has been. He's a world-class shooter, both off the catch and dribble, near and far. Going back to Cleveland, he has consistently ranked north of the 90th percentile as both a pick-and-roll and isolation scorer, per Synergy. What he's doing to start this season probably won't continue, but it also didn't come out of nowhere.

#2675. MLB rumors: Padres decline option on key rotation piece, Korean star to be posted

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The 2026-27 MLB offseason is only four days old and already the hot stove moves and rumors are coming in. Here are our top 50 free agents and top 25 trade candidates, and here are the important offseason dates and deadlines you need to know. Here now are Sunday's hot stove happenings.

San Diego's top two starters are now free agents. Two days after Michael King exercised an opt-out clause to become a free agent, the Padres declined their $14 million club option on Nick Pivetta, reports the San Diego Union-Tribune. Had the Padres picked up the option, Pivetta would have held an $18 million player option for 2028. That surely factored into the team's decision.

Pivetta, 34 in February, missed roughly five months with a flexor strain this past season. He returned late in the season and pitched reasonably well in six starts spanning September and the postseason. The San Diego Union-Tribune notes the Padres still have concerns about Pivetta's elbow, but could re-sign him to a new contract with a lower salary and/or no player option.

San Diego signed Pivetta to what amounted to a two-year, $23 million contact with two players options in February 2025. The flexor strain triggered an injury clause that converted the 2027 player option into a club option. We ranked Pivetta as the offseason's 43rd-best free agent.

As expected, the Orioles have declined their $20 million club option for center fielder Luis Robert Jr., reports ESPN. They will pay him a $2 million buyout, so it was functionally an $18 million decision. Robert suffered a hamstring injury and played only three games with the O's after being claimed off waivers from the Mets in late September.

Now 29, Robert again had multiple stints on the injured list this past season. He continued to punish lefties and play solid center field defense when healthy, but injuries have limited him to only 271 of 489 possible regular-season games from 2024-26. We did not rank Robert among our top 50 free agents, though he is an interesting upside play given his age.

The Hanwha Eagles of the Korea Baseball Organization will post star third baseman Si-Hwan Roh for MLB teams this offseason, reports Yonhap News Agency. Roh signed the richest deal in KBO history in February (11 years and $23 million), though as part of the deal, the Eagles agreed to post him this offseason, and Roh agreed to return to the team once his MLB stint is over.

Roh, 26, has been one of the KBO's best players the last several years. He hit .283/.360/.505 with 29 home runs in 2026, and has averaged 35 home runs per 162 games since 2023. Roh is considered a reliable but unspectacular defender at third, plus he has first base experience as well. This free agent class is very thin at the hot corner. Roh should generate a good deal of interest.

KBO players get a 30-day negotiating window once officially posted. If Roh does not sign with an MLB team during the 30-day window, he will return to the Eagles. It's possible that Roh, a right-handed hitter, will eclipse his $23 million guarantee with the Eagles over just a handful of years with an MLB team.

The Astros have acquired Triple-A righty reliever Evan Reifert from the Rays for cash, reports the Tampa Bay Times. Houston is likely to add him to their 40-man roster to protect him from the Rule 5 Draft. The Rays did not have the roster space to do that, so they traded for cash rather than lose him for nothing. Reifert, 27, has an excellent slider and used it to strike out 81 batters in 58 Triple-A innings in 2026. He should spend time in Houston's bullpen next season.

#2674. NHL Power Rankings: Oilers fly out of the starting gates behind Connor McDavid, Evan Bouchard

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

How many times in recent history have the Edmonton Oilers dug themselves an early hole only to surge back toward the top of the Pacific Division standings? It doesn't look like that surge will be necessary in 2026-27.

I had serious reservations about the Mike Babcock hire -- and I still do -- but Edmonton has been mauling opponents early. The Oilers are off to a 5-0-1 start while posting a plus-11 goal differential. Each of the team's wins has come by at least two goals.

As you might expect, Connor McDavid, Leon Draisaitl and Evan Bouchard are driving the bus in oil country. McDavid leads the NHL with 17 points, and Draisaitl is in double-digits with 11 points of his own, but Bouchard has been the star of the show early.

Bouchard has always been an offensive machine, but he's hit another level. He's tallied six goals and eight assists, and his 14 points leads all defensemen by a comfortable margin. The most impressive part of Bouchard's game to this point has been his five-on-five impacts. With Bouchard on the ice, the Oilers have outscored opponents 15-2, per Natural Stat Trick.

With Zach Hyman and Ryan Nugent-Hopkins out of the lineup, the Oilers haven't missed a beat thanks to its trio of superstars.

#2673. NBA Power Rankings: Warriors fly into top 10 with rejuvenated Stephen Curry, 76ers pushing for top spot

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After the Warriors' win over Phoenix on Monday, their fifth straight (something they never managed last season), Stephen Curry was asked what about this year's squad feels different from the one that finished with 37 wins a year ago.

"I mean, Yax," Curry laughed, stating the obvious when it comes to the historic start of Warriors' rookie Yaxel Lendeborg. "BP [Brandin Podziemski] taking another step forward. B-Will [Brandon Williams] has been great for us off the bench, giving us something we haven't had in a while. We've had some individual production that's been pretty cool, some standout guys who've made their presence felt night after night.

"But I think collectively," Curry continued, "we're probably a little bit more prepared on the details of what we're trying to do, and not just taking for granted that you can just play like the Warriors of old and expect good things to happen."

Curry didn't elaborate on these "details" on which the Warriors are more focused this season, but it looks about the same on the statistical surface. They're playing at the same pace. Making the same amount of 3s. They're still a high-turnover offense. They remain small, collectively old and not particularly athletic. They own a nearly identical 114-ish defensive rating, which at the moment has them ranked as a bottom-10 unit. Their spot-up, pick-and-roll, transition and isolation frequencies are all pretty much the same, per Synergy.

Which is to say, the Warriors are, in fact, playing like the Warriors. They look so good, that they've jumped 15 spots this week into the top 10 of our weekly NBA Power Rankings. Let's break down three reasons why.

Anyone who says they can see slippage in Curry's game must be looking through one hell of a high-powered microscope. He's scoring more than a point a minute (30 PPG in 28.8 MPG). The only other player doing that, with at least 100 minutes played, is Luka Dončić.

Get this: According to Cleaning the Glass, the 137.4 points that Curry is currently scoring per 100 shot attempts registers as a career high. He's taking more than 10 3-pointers a night and connecting at a 43% clip. On Monday, he finally missed a free throw after making 51 straight to start the year.

So yeah, Curry is still Curry. The difference is, he's got a real co-star again (remember, this team was tracking toward a conference finals trip when Jimmy Butler first came over) in the form a 24-year-old rookie.

Even knowing Curry's greatness, just about everyone pegged Golden State as a lottery team this year. They may still end up there, but at the moment Lendeborg has completely revived a team that we had all left for dead. He's the only rookie in history other than Larry Bird to post at least 100 points, 40 rebounds and 20 assists through his first five games. He's just the third player in Warriors history to average north of 20 PPG (22.3) over his first seven games of his career, joining Wilt Chamberlain and Rick Barry. In the win over the Clippers on Sunday, he became the fourth rookie in history log a game with at least 37 points and five assists on 85% true shooting.

Lendeborg is tracking toward Rookie of the Year and honest All-Star consideration. He has given the Warriors a legit first option without Curry on the court, and, in tandem, he massively eases Curry's burden as a creator. The guy is already a pick-and-roll machine and, at the moment, the most efficient isolation scorer in the league.

For some reason Podziemski has become a punching bag for a lot of Warriors fans, but he's been a winning player from day one (just go look at his on/off splits dating back to his rookie year). With Butler out, and until Lendeborg came along, Podziemski was the only Warrior other than Curry who could generate real paint pressure.

This season, Podziemski is putting it all together to the tune of a career-high 17 points, five assists and five boards per game. Once again, the splits tell the tale: The Warriors have outscored opponents by 50 points with Podziemski on the floor so far this year, by far the team high.

Suddenly the Warriors have three to four guys on any given night who can break a defense down, and with that you're seeing these support-staff guys like Georges Niang, Gui Santos, De'Anthony Melton, Gary Payton II, Will Richard, Al Horford, and even Charles Bassey (who has gone from taking DNPs to putting up 25 points and 18 boards over the last two games) to ride shotgun on a top-five offense.

#2672. Mets legend Jerry Koosman dies at 83: Pitcher helped New York win 1969 World Series

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Mets team Hall of Famer and two-time All-Star Jerry Koosman died Sunday morning in Osceola, Wisconsin, the team announced. He was 83. The Mets say Koosman battled multiple illnesses before his death.

"Kooz was one of the greatest pitchers in team history and a beloved member of the Mets family," Mets owners Alex and Steve Cohen said in a statement. "The 1969 Miracle Mets were filled with heroes, and the special southpaw from Appleton, Minnesota, was central to their success. He was a fierce competitor on the field, and respected teammate in the clubhouse. His legendary performance in the World Series helped the Mets secure their first Championship in team history. On behalf of the entire Mets organization, we extend our heartfelt condolences to Jerry's family, friends, former teammates and all who loved him."

The Mets discovered Koosman while he was pitching for the United States Army and signed him to a contract in August 1964. He made his MLB debut in April 1967 and moved into the rotation full-time the next season. Koosman threw 263 ⅔ innings with a 2.08 ERA as a rookie in 1968, which earned him an All-Star Game selection and MVP votes, and a second-place finish in the Rookie of the Year voting behind Hall of Famer Johnny Bench.

In 1969, Koosman was again an All-Star, throwing 241 innings with a 2.28 ERA. He was New York's No. 2 starter in the postseason between Hall of Famers Tom Seaver and Nolan Ryan. Koosman made two starts for the Miracle Mets in the World Series, including the Game 5 clincher against the Baltimore Orioles. He allowed three runs in the complete game win and recorded all but one possible out in his two World Series starts.

From 1968-76, Koosman was simply one of the best pitchers in the game, pitching to a 2.94 ERA and averaging 223 innings per season. The Mets traded him to the Minnesota Twins for Jesse Orosco in December 1978 and Koosman finished his career with stints for the Twins (1979-81), Chicago White Sox (1981-83), and Philadelphia Phillies (1984-85).

Koosman retired following the 1985 season with a 222-209 record and a 3.36 ERA that is 39th among AL/NL pitchers with at least 3,500 career innings. He ranks 35th all-time in strikeouts (2,556), 40th all-time in starts (527), 48th all-time in innings (3,839 ⅓), and 77th all-time in pitching WAR (57.0). Koosman went to two All-Star Games and finished second to Randy Jones in the 1976 Cy Young voting.

The Mets inducted Koosman into their Hall of Fame in 1989 and retired his No. 36 in 2021. His 140 wins are the most in franchise history among left-handers and third in team history overall, behind Seaver (198) and Dwight Gooden (157). Koosman is second in Mets history in innings (behind Seaver) and third in strikeouts (behind Seaver and Gooden).

Koosman fell off the Baseball Writers Association of America's Hall of Fame ballot in 1991, his first year of eligibility.

#2669. Houston Rockets centers Steven Adam and Clint Capela expected to return next week

The Houston Rockets have good news and bad news at the center position.

The good news: Steven Adams and Clint Capela, who have missed the last eight and three games, respectively, are expected back soon. Coach Ime Udoka said Monday that the team was targeting either the Nov. 15 game at the Washington Wizards or the Nov. 16 contest at the Miami Heat for their returns.

Adams, one of the league's best offensive rebounders, missed Houston's season opener with a right calf soreness/tightness, returned to play a little over eight minutes in the second game and hasn't played since with a right soleus (back calf muscle) strain. Capela rolled his ankle on Halloween against the Oklahoma City Thunder.

The bad news? Those absences combined with Oscar Tshiebwe missing Monday's game against the Denver Nuggets due to illness - Udoka said hopefully a one-game absence - meant the Rockets were to face three-time MVP Nikola Jokic with just one healthy center, Alperen Şengün. Jokic is averaging 22.9 points, 10.1 rebounds and 9.1 assists per game, relatively down numbers for him.

"Play some small ball," Udoka said pregame when asked how Houston planned to deal with Jokic. "We have some wings with size and some rugged guys down there that can battle a little bit. … We're very comfortable going small, although Jokic is a tough task for bigs alone, and so we'll mix up some coverages and schemes."

Udoka listed Jabari Smith Jr., Marcus Smart and Jae'Sean Tate when asked who would guard Jokic, saying that they'll try to deny some catches or push the center's catch point out to the perimeter.

Here are the game's best defenders in 2026 according to Statcast's Fielding Runs Value, an all-encompassing metric that factors in range and arm, as well as blocking and framing for catchers:

Gold Gloves have be awarded since 1957 and are given to the best defensive player at each position in each league. That first year was one MLB-wide honor at each position. In 1958, Gold Gloves were split into AL and NL. Also, it used to be three outfielders per league regardless of exact position. Now the outfield spots are broken down into left field, center field, and right field.

Winners are determined through manager/coach voting (75%) and a statistical component (25%). Team employees can not vote for their own players.

While MLB announced "finalists" for each Gold Glove a few weeks back, remember that the voting was already complete and those finalists were simply the top three vote-getters at each position. #2666. Warriors reportedly aren't paying Kristaps Porziņģis as former All-Star combats health issues

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Golden State Warriors are withholding payments to Kristaps Porziņģis on his $20 million salary as he remains away from the team, according to ESPN. Porziņģis signed a two-year, $40 million contract with the Warriors over the summer that included a $3 million guarantee for the 2027-28 season. However, to this point, he has not been able to suit up for the Warriors as he has dealt with undisclosed health problems. Porziņģis has reportedly considered stepping away from basketball altogether, but has not publicized any decisions. Porziņģis does not currently plan to challenge the Warriors on this decision, according to The Athletic.

A spokesperson for the National Basketball Players Association declined to comment when reached by CBS Sports.

Porziņģis has been dealing with health issues since the end of his tenure with the Boston Celtics. He previously disclosed a diagnosis of POTS, or postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, but that diagnosis appears to be in some dispute. Warriors coach Steve Kerr said in a radio interview earlier this year that Atlanta Hawks general manager Onsi Saleh "said it's not actually POTS," but then walked back his comments a few days later.

Porziņģis has been away from the team since late September. He met with general manager Mike Dunleavy and vice president of player health and performance Rick Celebrini in mid-October; after that meeting, the Warriors announced that he would be "around the team," but that has thus far not been the case, at least publicly.

Porziņģis released the following statement on his health in October, later adding, specifically, that he does not have HIV or AIDS.

"Hello people, I'm working with doctors and experts to figure out how to be fully back to good health asap. Honestly, I'm getting better and better. I just have to stay patient, and I believe I'll be feeling great again soon," Porziņģis wrote. "It has definitely been frustrating dealing with some health stuff that you can't exactly pinpoint, on top of injuries throughout my career, so it has added up for sure, but we will get through it. Health is wealth. Thank you for all the support."

NBA players are typically paid regardless of health status, but teams will occasionally withhold salary if they believe the player is in breach of contract. The most notable example occurred between Ben Simmons and the Philadelphia 76ers during the 2021-22 season, when Simmons wanted to be traded. The 76ers maintained that Simmons refused to play in regular-season games and failed to show up for the start of training camp, but Simmons cited his mental health as the reason for his limited engagement with the team. Simmons was eventually traded to the Brooklyn Nets, and he and the 76ers agreed to a settlement that saw Simmons recoup a portion of the withheld salary.

The Warriors are attempting to trade Porziņģis in an effort to utilize his $20 million cap figure. While he would not have trade value as a player given his health status, he is essentially an expiring contract with only that small $3 million guarantee on the books for next season. That could potentially make him valuable to a team looking to move off of longer-term money, or the Warriors could entice another team into a trade using draft picks with Porziņģis serving only as the matching salary.

Golden State has gotten off to a surprisingly successful 5-3 start this season despite Porziņģis' absence, thanks in large part to the stellar performance of Stephen Curry and the emergence of rookie Yaxel Lendeborg as a foundational player. On paper, Porziņģis is exactly the sort of player this roster needs: a center who can shoot 3-pointers to complement Draymond Green, a poor shooting power forward. As it grows increasingly unlikely that Porziņģis will ever suit up for Golden State again, though, a trade is the only real path the Warriors have to making the best of a bad situation.

As our own Isaac Trotter explains, if Haugh can improve his range shooting, he won't have to wait long to hear his name called in the 2027 NBA Draft.

When it comes to how the talent broke down by conference, it was a a pretty level playing field for the most part.

Not to spoil anyting, but Arizona freshman Caleb Holt did not make the cut. He did, however, turn some heads in the Wildcats' exhibition game.

Loyalty is an excellent quality to have in a friend or partner. It's also why we love dogs.

It should not be quite as prevalent among college football coaches, some of whom have been undone because they did what was comfortable, not what was necessarily best for the team.

Our own John Talty highlighted five high-profile coaches who have been loyal to a fault, making hires and personnel decisions that have come back to haunt them. One of those coaches is Mike Elko. After a shaky season from Marcel Reed in 2025, Texas A&M chose not to pursue an upgrade in the portal.

Instead, the Aggies gave Reed a major payday, and they'll miss the College Football Playoff because of it.

Look, it can happen to the best of us. Dan Lanning and Dabo Swinney wound up on the list, despite the success that those two have had throughout their careers.

Steve Sarkisian is another coach who has fallen into the trap of being too loyal, but he may have a huge decision on his hands in the offseason. Arch Manning has struggled enough that another year in college should be on the table. If that happens, would Sark welcome back Manning with open arms, despite his shortcomings?

Finally, one person for whom loyalty is no an issue is Missouri QB Austin Simmons. After Trinidad Chambliss won the starting job at Ole Miss last year, Simmons didn't feel the need to stick around, but there won't be bitterness when Simmons returns to Oxford this weekend.

#2664. MLB Power Rankings: Brewers end 2026 season at No. 1 as World Series champions

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I'm done. No more. Enough is enough. I have doubted the Brewers far too many times and I decided in early August to never do it again. I started picking them to win the World Series every chance I got. I was finally right.

Every time they traded away someone good (the latest being Freddy Peralta last offseason), I thought, "OK, now is when it finally catches up with them." Only it never does. I thought they needed Tarik Skubal, both to reinforce their rotation and also to keep him away from the Dodgers. It didn't matter. They beat him and swept the Dodgers in the NLCS.

It's a juggernaut of an organization. They churn out talent and get the most out of every player they have. They seem to trade away talent at the exact right time. They develop young stars better than anyone. There's another one coming in Jesús Made, but there's no reason for Brewers fans to dream about the future when the present is World Series champions.

Jackson Chourio is becoming a superstar, Jacob Misiorowski is going to win the National League Cy Young and Christian Yelich is a former MVP, but it isn't really about the big names with this group. It's everything. It's the entire team making this train run, working as a cohesive unit. It's Robert Gasser going out and dealing in Game 3 after starting the season in the minors. It's Jake Bauers winning NLCS MVP not too long after he was ready to retire from baseball. It's Aaron Ashby putting up one of the greatest reliever performances in playoff history. It's Sal Frelick hitting a game-tying bomb. It's Cooper Pratt's coming-out party in the World Series. And on and on and on we could go.

Milwaukee is the best organization in baseball now, supplanting the former two-time defending champion Dodgers.

The Brewers head to next season with plenty of question marks, but they'll answer them. They always do. They are the champions of Major League Baseball and they sit atop the final 2026 Power Rankings.

Looking forward to next spring, my expectation is the Brewers will be No. 1. Some years, I write about why the defending champion is not No. 1. I've long since learned my lesson with this team, though. No more. The Brewers will be No. 1 heading into spring training.
